messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Waiter/Waitress
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh is a 48-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who works as a waitress at a mid-sized family restaurant in her city. She is divorced and lives alone. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician, and she arrived at the intake appointment guarded, speaking quietly and rarely making eye contact.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Linh became aware that a man she had briefly dated was following her. What began as repeated appearances at her restaurant — sitting in her section, watching her move between tables — escalated over several months into notes left on her car, phone calls at 2 a.m., and on one occasion, the discovery that he had been standing outside her apartment building for hours. The stalking reached its peak on a night when she returned home from a closing shift to find her front door unlocked. She did not know whether he had been inside. She stood in the doorway for what she later described as a very long time, unable to move or speak. Police involvement eventually led to a restraining order, but by then the damage, as Linh understood it, was already done.

In the weeks that followed, something in Linh's memory of those months refused to settle into ordinary recollection. She finds that she cannot put what happened into coherent language — when she tries to describe the period to anyone, including her therapist, the words do not arrive in the right order, and what she produces feels disconnected from anything she recognises as herself. The memory, she says, feels like it belongs to a different woman entirely. And yet it does not stay at a distance: it forces itself into her mind without warning, most often when she is mid-task at work — carrying plates, taking an order — and the intrusion leaves her physically shaken, heart hammering, skin flushed. These unbidden returns of the experience feed directly into how she now understands her life: she has come to believe that the woman she was before — someone she remembers as genuinely happy, someone who found pleasure in small things — is simply gone. Nothing in her days feels meaningful. She describes herself as feeling dead inside, a phrase she returns to with a flatness that suggests it is not metaphor but diagnosis.

This profound sense of inner loss has in turn shaped how vigilantly she monitors the world around her. Because she has concluded that safety is no longer something she can take for granted, she listens for sounds at night — footsteps in the hallway, the particular creak of the building's entrance — and she avoids any place she has not been before, reasoning that unfamiliar environments offer no baseline against which to detect danger. At the restaurant, this plays out concretely: she has quietly arranged her sections so that she works only the tables nearest the kitchen, where she can see both the entrance and the back exit simultaneously. When a new customer sits in an unfamiliar part of the floor, she finds reasons to ask a colleague to cover. The hypervigilance is exhausting, and its exhaustion deepens her conviction that her life has become unrecognisable.

The sense of permanent diminishment and the constant state of alert together drive a set of strategies that have narrowed her world considerably. She avoids the friends she socialised with before the stalking began — seeing them, she fears, would require her to account for who she has become, and she cannot bear that reflection. Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation she sidesteps entirely, even minor ones at work, because conflict now registers in her body as threat. She has also begun to avoid looking at or touching her own body, as though it too is a site she no longer trusts. These withdrawals, over the months, have had the effect of sealing off the very contexts in which the memory might be processed or spoken — without social contact, without embodied presence, without the friction of ordinary disagreement, there is nothing to interrupt the memory's uncontrolled returns, and so it continues to arrive uninvited, sustaining the dread and the emptiness in equal measure.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a shift at the restaurant last month in which she froze completely when a male customer raised his voice at a colleague near her station. She stood holding a tray, unable to move, until a coworker touched her arm. She is most afraid, she says, that this is simply who she is now. What she is hoping for, though she offers it tentatively, is to feel something again.
